A.explanation: This statement is true - moving source or observer changes observed frequency for both sound, e.g. ambulance siren, and light, e.g. red shift - so it is not the required answer.

B.explanation: This statement is true - light oscillations are perpendicular to travel and can be polarised, while sound oscillations are parallel to travel in air - so it is not the required answer.

C.explanation: This statement is false - diffraction is a property of all progressive waves, and sound diffracts strongly round doorways while light diffracts through narrow slits.

D.explanation: This statement is true - light is an electromagnetic wave needing no medium, while sound needs particles to transmit compressions and rarefactions - so it is not the required answer.

hints: Notice the question asks for the statement that is not correct, so three options describe true shared or contrasting behaviour of light and sound.
Recall that transverse versus longitudinal describes oscillation direction, vacuum travel describes need for a medium, and Doppler effect describes motion-induced frequency shift.
Recall that diffraction is spreading after a gap or obstacle when wavelength is similar to gap size, and check whether this applies only to light or to sound with its much larger wavelength as well.
walkthrough: Identify the task: test each statement about light waves as electromagnetic transverse waves and sound waves as mechanical longitudinal waves for truth, then select the false one.

Check Doppler effect: relative motion of source and observer changes observed wavefront spacing and hence frequency for any wave, observed for sound pitch and for light wavelength shift, so A is correct physics.

Check wave type and medium: light has electric and magnetic field oscillations transverse to propagation and travels at $3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in vacuum, while sound has air pressure oscillations parallel to propagation and cannot travel without a medium, so B and D are correct physics.

Check diffraction: all waves diffract and spread when passing a gap of width comparable to wavelength $\lambda$, which is easily seen for sound of $\lambda \approx 1 \text{ m}$ at doorways and also occurs for light of $\lambda \approx 500 \text{ nm}$ at narrow slits.
Therefore the claim that sound waves cannot be diffracted is false and is the not correct statement. This is option C.
